source.title: A Conflict of Visions: Ideological Origins of Political Struggles

learning_objectives.2.1: Contrast how the two visions conceive human nature: an inherent egocentricity to be worked within — moral and social benefits produced by incentives rather than changed dispositions — versus a circumstantial selfishness that a “perfectible” (continually improvable, never perfect) man can outgrow, which makes incentives unworthy expedients.
learning_objectives.2.2: Explain why the constrained vision can hope only for trade-offs — every restraint on inherent human evils carries costs of its own, so prudence is “the first of all virtues” and ideals are weighed against their cost — while the unconstrained vision seeks solutions that end the need for trade-offs and treats process costs as regrettable but not decisive.
learning_objectives.2.3: Explain why intentions are decisive in the unconstrained vision yet nearly irrelevant in the constrained one — Godwin's virtue/vice/negligence scheme has no cell for the unintended benefit at the centre of Smith's Wealth of Nations — so that one vision states its goals as desired results and the other as process characteristics.
learning_objectives.2.4: Explain why the two visions look in opposite places for causes: where evils are the default state of limited man, the constrained vision seeks the special causes of peace, wealth, and order; where man is not inherently limited, the unconstrained vision seeks the special causes of war, poverty, and crime in institutions and foolish choices.
learning_objectives.2.5: Predict, from one unfamiliar argument or policy stance, the position its holder's vision implies on a different issue — placing the stance by whether human limitations are built into its structure or treated as removable, not by how much it speaks of limits or potential.

Chapter 2 → The Nature of Man.text: One vision treats human egocentricity as a permanent fact to be worked within: benefits are produced by incentives, honour and moral principle rather than by remaking people, and what matters is how we act, not what we spontaneously feel. The other treats present selfishness as circumstantial and man as perfectible — continually improvable, with no limit anyone can specify — so contrived rewards look like unworthy expedients standing in the way of doing right because it is right.

Chapter 2 → Trade-offs Versus Solutions.text: Where human failings are inherent, every device that restrains them carries costs of its own, so nothing is available but trade-offs and prudence ranks first among virtues; ideals are weighed against what they cost, and the reformer aims at the best people can bear. Where failings are removable, a solution can end the need to trade off at all — and that prospect is what licenses transitional costs, which are regrettable without being decisive.

Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social C.text: Sorting acts into intended and unintended benefit and harm leaves one square empty — unintended benefit — and that empty square is where an entire economics sits: gains to society that formed no part of anyone's purpose. So one vision judges by intentions and names its goals as results it wants; the other judges by systemic characteristics. Each also finds the opposite thing puzzling: one hunts the causes of war and poverty, the other the causes of peace and wealth.

Chapter 2 → Summary and Implications.text: What places a thinker is not how often he speaks of human limits or of untapped potential, but whether those limits are built into the structure of his argument or treated as something institutions imposed and reform can remove. Someone may concede a limit freely and still refuse to let it constrain his conclusions. Because the starting picture of human nature shapes everything downstream, one stated position lets you predict the rest.

items.stem: In Adam Smith's example, a European who hears that an earthquake has swallowed up China soon returns to his business, though the loss of his own little finger would cost him a night's sleep. According to the chapter, what did Smith conclude about the project of changing this egocentric nature?
options: That it was the central moral task: the European's indifference showed a failure of education that a better upbringing could and should correct.
That it was possible but costly: the European's indifference was the work of artificial passions and social customs that had corrupted natural man.
That it was desirable but premature: under the current state of things, incentives would have to serve until dispositions could be reformed.
That it was vain and pointless: making the European feel the full pain of the Chinese would be perfectly useless, except to make him miserable.

items.stem: True or false: According to the chapter, Godwin conceded that, as things stand, people commonly prefer a lesser interest of their own to a greater interest of others.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter reports that Godwin and Condorcet held man to be 'perfectible.' According to the chapter, what did they mean by this?
options: That man can be brought to a state of actual, absolute perfection, after which no further moral improvement would be needed or possible for the species.
That man can be improved without limit, provided the right system of rewards and punishments is kept in place to reshape his existing habits over time.
That man can be improved only up to a definite ceiling, which reason can specify in advance and beyond which no progress is possible.
That man can be improved continually, coming nearer and nearer to an ideal with no limit anyone can prescribe, yet never reaching perfection.

items.stem: Smith relied on a system of moral and economic incentives to draw benefits for others out of self-centered men. According to the chapter, why did Godwin disdain such socially contrived incentives?
options: Because he held that inducements addressed to honor, nobility, and moral principle, rather than to economic self-interest, were the only ones worthy of a rational being.
Because he doubted that incentives could move existing men at all, so deeply had prejudice, artificial passion, and social custom corrupted them beyond the reach of any reward or punishment.
Because he thought incentives might have to serve for the present, but only until education had reformed dispositions far enough to make such expedients safe to discard.
Because selfishness arose from circumstances, not from our nature, so people could do right because it is right; rewards only fostered the selfishness they were meant to curb.

items.stem: The chapter says that, for Smith, people on many occasions sacrifice their own interests to the greater interests of others. According to the chapter, how did Smith reconcile this with his picture of an egocentric human nature?
options: The feeling is egocentric, but we cannot prefer ourselves so shamelessly when we act; devices such as honor and moral principle get the sacrifice made.
Nature, having loaded us with our own sorrows, also planted a love of our neighbor as ourselves, and this sentiment moves us to their relief when their need is greater.
Man can directly feel other people's needs as more important than his own, and so can act impartially even when his own interests are involved.
Egocentricity belongs only to the current state of things; as a higher sense of social duty develops in the long run, such sacrifices become a natural inclination.

items.stem: In Sowell's account of the unconstrained vision, what precisely counts as a 'solution'?
options: A remedy whose expected benefits have been carefully weighed against the full costs of bringing it about
A state in which a trade-off is no longer necessary, even if reaching it entailed costs that are now past
The best arrangement that the people can be brought to bear, given their confirmed habits and prejudices
The most immediately effective incentive available under the current state of things, whatever men's dispositions

items.stem: According to Sowell, why can the constrained vision hope for no more than 'a prudent trade-off' in dealing with evils such as war, poverty and crime?
options: Because the natural constraints of food and death set a ceiling that no social arrangement can lift, whatever human nature turns out to be
Because sufficient moral commitment to solve them has never yet been mustered, though nothing intractable stands in the way of doing so
Because the special causes of war, poverty and crime have yet to be discovered, so any remedy must remain provisional until they are found
Because whatever restrains inherent human evils has costs of its own, including other social ills that the civilizing institutions create

items.stem: A defender of legal technicalities that let some criminals escape punishment says, 'That is the price we pay for freedom.' In Sowell's reading, which vision does the remark express, and why?
options: The constrained vision, since the speaker openly concedes that freedom carries a real cost for society
The constrained vision, since the speaker accepts an imperfect legal institution rather than trying to perfect it
The unconstrained vision, since the speaker expects the technicalities to be reformed away once wiser policies prevail
The unconstrained vision, since the cost is named only to be treated as secondary to the ideal it serves

items.stem: True or false: in Sowell's account, a 'prudent reformer' who respects the people's confirmed habits and prejudices and seeks to establish 'the best that the people can bear' leans toward the unconstrained vision, since he aims to improve society rather than leave it as it is.
options: True
False

items.stem: Sowell notes that prudence — the careful weighing of trade-offs — is 'among the highest duties' in the constrained vision but 'of a lower order of importance' in the unconstrained vision. Why the difference?
options: Because moral improvement has no fixed limit in the unconstrained vision, so a solution can supersede the trade-offs that prudence weighs
Because the unconstrained vision looks to incentives rather than to judgment to steer men toward good deeds, which makes prudence redundant
Because the unconstrained vision denies that social change carries any costs, which leaves prudence nothing to weigh against the ideal
Because the unconstrained vision treats intentions as decisive, and prudence is a matter of calculating consequences rather than of meaning well

items.stem: Sowell observes that Godwin's classification of human actions left one kind of action without any category. Which kind was it, and why does Sowell single out the omission?
options: Careless harm — the category on which Smith's account of capitalists relied
Intended harm — the category Smith found in capitalists' conspiracies against the public
Unintended benefit — the category on which Smith's Wealth of Nations turned
Intended benefit — the category Smith dismissed as scarcely worth noticing
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell indicates that, within the constrained vision, what chiefly recommends a policy is the sincerity and dedication of the people who advance it.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell notes that Adam Smith characterized the capitalist's intentions as 'mean rapacity' and described capitalists as conspiring against the public whenever they met — yet Smith became the patron saint of laissez-faire capitalism. According to Sowell, why is there no contradiction?
options: For Smith, capitalists' rapacity was a regrettable cost of the process, outweighed by the prosperity laissez-faire was meant to deliver.
For Smith, the harsh portraits were rhetorical excess; his considered view was that most capitalists genuinely intended the public good.
For Smith, competition would gradually refine capitalists' dispositions until their motives came to coincide with the public good.
For Smith, social benefit came from the systemic characteristics of a competitive economy, not from the intentions of anyone within it.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell notes that, in The Wealth of Nations, economic benefits to society were largely unintended by individuals and emerged systemically from the marketplace. Which statement correctly describes how, in Sowell's account, that process connects individual self-interest to the interest of society?
options: The process gradually replaces self-centred motives with a genuine disposition to serve the needs of others directly.
The process simply adds up the separate self-interests of individuals, and their sum turns out to be the interest of society.
The process requires each individual to do things for other people; only the motivation behind those acts is self-centred.
The process brings self-interest and the social interest into identity, so that no trade-off between them remains necessary.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell says the two visions do not merely have different goals; their goals 'relate to different things.' Which statement best explains what he means?
options: The unconstrained vision sets its goals for a distant future; the constrained vision confines its goals to what the present generation can use.
The unconstrained vision seeks results for society as a whole; the constrained vision seeks results for particular individuals and particular groups.
The unconstrained vision names the results it wants; the constrained vision names the features of a process it expects to be conducive to results.
The unconstrained vision states its goals in moral terms; the constrained vision states them in economic terms, as returns weighed against costs.
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: In Sowell's account, it is believers in the constrained vision — not the unconstrained — who seek the special causes of peace, wealth, and a law-abiding society.
options: True
False
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell says the writers of The Federalist Papers were quite conscious of the vision of man underlying the Constitution's elaborate checks and balances. In his reading, what did they take such institutions to be?
options: Chains that narrow and corrupt a nature born free and innocent
Ways of trying to cope with an evil inherent in man himself
Counterweights that needlessly complicate the machine and weigh upon the people
Devices to be retired once all citizens were devoted to their country and its laws
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell writes that believers in the unconstrained vision seek the special causes of war, poverty, and crime, while believers in the constrained vision seek the special causes of peace, wealth, and a law-abiding society. Why, in his account, does the constrained vision look in that direction?
options: Because it holds that dwelling on social evils only tempts reformers toward the utopian solutions that do more harm than the evils themselves
Because it regards war, poverty, and crime as so deeply rooted in human nature that explaining them would serve no practical purpose
Because it takes those evils to follow from man's own limitations and passions, so that it is their absence which calls for explanation
Because it traces those evils to failed institutions and rulers, whose particular failures no general account of human nature can explain
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell uses the exchange between Malthus and Godwin over population to make a point about the two visions. In his account, what did the two men actually disagree about?
options: Their pictures of human nature — whether people would needlessly multiply until subsistence became hard to achieve
Their pictures of nature itself — whether the need for food is a genuine constraint or an artifact of injurious institutions
Their view of nature's bounty — whether cultivation could raise the food supply as fast as human numbers could grow
Their arithmetic — whether a geometrical increase in population was possible, or merely a rhetorical device of Malthus's
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: Sowell notes that the French Revolution gave sweeping powers, including the power of life and death, to those who spoke in the name of the people — and that when its believers were bitterly disappointed in particular leaders, they deposed and executed them and carried on much as before. In his reading, what does that response reveal about the causal logic of the unconstrained vision?
options: It accepts the revolution's bloodshed as a regrettable cost, secondary to the solution being pursued
It locates the evil in the persons who betrayed the cause, not in the system that had empowered them
It holds that no one is ever to be completely trusted with power, so power must be checked by opposing powers
It treats the passions of men as unable to conform to reason and justice without external constraint
items.source_anchor: Chapter 2 → Social Morality and Social Causation

items.stem: According to the chapter's summary, what determines whether a thinker belongs to the constrained or to the unconstrained tradition?
options: Whether the thinker holds that human nature is wholly fixed or wholly changeable
Whether the thinker's proposals defend existing institutions or seek to replace them
Whether constraints are built into the structure and operation of the theory
Whether the thinker refers more often to human limitations than to human potential

items.stem: In Sowell's account, Rousseau's claim that man is born free but is everywhere in chains expresses the unconstrained vision.
options: True
False

items.stem: Condorcet acknowledged that human intelligence has limits, yet Sowell places him among the clearest exemplars of the unconstrained vision. What, in Sowell's account, keeps that acknowledgment from making his vision a constrained one?
options: He granted that a limit exists but held that no one could say where it lies
He granted the limit for isolated individuals but denied it for the whole species
He treated the limit as a fact of external nature rather than of human nature
He referred to human potential far more often than to human limitations

items.stem: A commentator defends legal technicalities that occasionally let a guilty person go free with the words, "That is the price we pay for freedom." Sowell files this with the unconstrained vision. Which reading explains the placement?
options: The cost is acknowledged and then denied any decisive weight against the ideal
The speaker treats freedom as a fixed limit that no reform could remove
The speaker is defending existing institutions rather than seeking to change them
The speaker weighs freedom's benefits against the cost and finds them larger

items.stem: Dana runs operations for a hospital chain. Urging the board to scrap its incident-reporting scheme of points, penalties and a league table, she says: "Let's be realistic about human nature. Put people under a scoreboard and they will bury mistakes, shift blame and protect their numbers — that is exactly what our staff have learned to do. Take the scoreboard away and the candor you find in any good clinical team comes back on its own." The chain has just bought a hospital abroad, where staff hand patients over between shifts by a long-standing local custom. On whether the chain's standard handover protocol should be adjusted to that custom, which position does Dana's vision imply?
options: Adapt the protocol to the local custom
Keep the existing local custom instead
Introduce the protocol as written
Let the local staff decide

items.stem: Marta chairs a city transit board and opens every meeting by reminding colleagues that the budget is finite and that riders are not saints. Backing a plan to make every bus and train fare-free, she gives most of her memo to the downside: fares are a third of the budget, service will thin for years, two outer neighborhoods will lose their routes, and some riders will abuse a free system. She closes: "I have hidden none of this, and it is heavy. None of it is a reason to go on running a city where a person can be priced off a bus." Marta is later asked about a puzzle in the county's schools: one district has held its dropout rate near zero for a decade while every district around it has watched dropouts climb. Which line of inquiry does Marta's vision imply she would take up first?
options: Whether that district simply counts dropouts differently
Why the surrounding districts are losing students
What that district's near-zero rate is costing it elsewhere
How that district has managed to hold on to its students

source.title: A Conflict of Visions: Ideological Origins of Political Struggles

learning_objectives.3.1: Explain how each vision's definition of knowledge — unarticulated experience distilled into habits, prices, and traditions in the constrained vision, explicitly articulated reason in the unconstrained — determines whether knowledge is seen as widely dispersed among the many or concentrated in a few cultivated minds.
learning_objectives.3.2: Explain why the unconstrained vision looks to those with special articulated knowledge — intellectuals and the articulate young — as guides for social improvement, and why the constrained vision, while conceding their narrow expertise, denies them any general superiority over the systemic processes that coordinate knowledge scattered among the many.
learning_objectives.3.3: Apply the distinction between articulated and systemic rationality — reason as a justification an actor can specify, versus reason as a cause that operates whether or not any participant can state it — to a new domain, determining whether the wisdom of an outcome lies in the actors' explicit reasoning or in the process itself.
learning_objectives.3.4: Explain how each vision frames the conflict over judicial activism — the unconstrained vision as one set of contemporaries against another, the constrained vision as the experience of many generations against the articulated reasoning of one contemporary school — and why, for the constrained side, the question is not which group is wiser but whether systemic experience is wiser than both.
learning_objectives.3.5: Given a person in an entrusted role — judge, executive, scholar, journalist, or a role the chapter never names — determine what each vision holds to be that person's best contribution to the social good: directly shaping the outcome they sincerely judge best, or faithfully discharging the role's defined duties and leaving outcomes to the systemic process.
learning_objectives.3.6: Explain why sincerity is central to the unconstrained vision and of minor weight in the constrained vision, and what follows for how each side treats adversaries and truth — including why, within the unconstrained vision, Godwin's omnipotent reason forbids deception and force while Lenin's frictions make them duties.

Chapter 3 → The Mobilization of Knowledg.text: One vision counts as knowledge the whole store of experience carried in habits, prices and traditions — much of it never put into words, winnowed over generations by what worked — so it lies scattered among everyone. The other counts only what can be stated and reasoned explicitly, which concentrates it in cultivated minds. Because they mean different things by the word, they disagree about where knowledge sits, and therefore about whose judgment should govern.

Chapter 3 → Articulated Versus Systemic.text: Reason means two things: a cause that operates whether or not anyone can state it, and a justification someone can spell out on demand. The more limited a vision thinks human capacity, the wider the gap between them. Where rationality is systemic, prices and practices adjust without any participant knowing how his response affects the whole; the pattern can be analyzed without being specifiable in enough detail for anyone to direct it, so how rational individuals are matters little.

Chapter 3 → Law.text: One side reads a legal dispute as a contest between two sets of living contemporaries, or at most between the living and one dead generation whose claims expire. The other reads it as a contest between two whole processes: experience accumulated across many generations, voiced by people alive now, against the explicit reasoning of one present-day school. On that second reading the question is not which group is wiser, but whether accumulated experience is wiser than either.

Chapter 3 → Social Policy.text: Where the wise are thought competent to shape outcomes, they should do so in whatever falls within their reach — the judge asking whether a result is good, the executive steering the firm toward what society needs. Where they are not, each person's best contribution is to discharge the duties of his own role and leave outcomes to the process; a specialist's advantage holds only inside a narrow range. Failures then read as symptoms of tinkering, not correctable slips.

Chapter 3 → Sincerity Versus Fidelity.text: If an individual can work out what is best for society, his sincerity matters enormously and is not lightly granted to opponents, whose real motives get unmasked instead. If he cannot, sincerity is cheap to concede — the sincere can still do great harm — and what counts is faithfulness to the duties of his role. Within the first view, how much resistance reason expects decides whether deception becomes forbidden or obligatory.

Chapter 3 → Youth and Age.text: If knowledge is accumulated experience, the young cannot rival the old: prudence is its fruit, and it is acquired wisdom that teaches you not to be credulous. If knowledge is what current schooling can impart, a young person today may carry more of it than the great minds of an earlier century — and being least settled into existing institutions and beliefs, the young become the natural agents of change rather than its likeliest casualties.

Chapter 3 → Summary and Implications.text: How widely knowledge is spread depends on what counts as knowledge. Define it to include the vast unspoken store summarized in habits, aversions and attractions, and it is everywhere; restrict it to what has been carefully articulated, and it belongs to a few. So one vision leans on evolved processes to gather and coordinate what no one person holds, while the other sees in unusual intellectual skill both its proof and its instrument of improvement.

items.stem: According to the chapter, why do the two visions reach such different conclusions about whether knowledge is concentrated in a few minds or dispersed among the many?
options: They disagree about whether existing institutions ought to be preserved or reformed
They disagree about whether experts really know more than laymen in their own fields
They disagree about how far formal education has spread through the population
They disagree about what kind of thing counts as knowledge in the first place

items.stem: In the unconstrained vision, because knowledge is defined as explicitly articulated reason, knowledge tends to be seen as spread more broadly through society than the constrained vision allows.
options: True
False

items.stem: Hayek held that, compared with the totality of knowledge a civilization continually uses, the difference between what the wisest and what the most ignorant individual can deliberately employ is 'comparatively insignificant.' Within the constrained vision, what makes that claim follow from its conception of knowledge?
options: What passes for expert knowledge is mostly fashionable and insignificant words that add nothing real to what the common man knows
Most knowledge is unarticulated experience held in habits and institutions, so what any person deliberately uses is a sliver
Schooling has now spread so widely that ordinary people command nearly all of what the experts themselves know
People differ so little in native ability that no one can outreason anyone else by more than a narrow and trivial margin

items.stem: Godwin dismissed 'the pretense of collective wisdom' as 'the most palpable of all impostures' and looked instead to the 'cultivated mind.' Which feature of the unconstrained vision's conception of knowledge leads it to locate knowledge in a few such minds rather than across the many?
options: It holds that persons of narrow views are inherently unable to rise to the level of the enlightened
It regards the expertise of specialists as confined to one narrow slice of human understanding
It treats the accumulated experience of past generations as the surest test of any belief
It counts as knowledge only what has been explicitly articulated and brought to the test of reason

items.stem: Burke was 'afraid to put men to live and trade each on his own private stock of reason,' because he suspected that 'this stock in each man is small.' Given how the constrained vision conceives knowledge, where does that smallness imply knowledge is to be found?
options: In the established institutions of the present day, which are to be preserved just as they currently stand
In a shared fund of experience built by nations and ages, spread across the many rather than held by a few
In the articulated findings of trained experts, who alone can validate what the many merely accept on habit
In the few minds whose stock of reason has been cultivated far enough to exceed that of the ordinary run of men

items.stem: Why does the unconstrained vision hold that the best conduct of social affairs depends on the few guiding the many?
options: Knowledge, conceived as accumulated experience, is most fully distilled in the few who have studied the wisdom of the ages
Intellectuals, having no particular interest to defend, are the only members of society whose sincerity can be relied on
Knowledge, conceived as explicitly articulated reason, is special and concentrated rather than widely shared
Intellectuals hold the institutional roles whose faithful discharge serves the systemic process that settles outcomes

items.stem: In the unconstrained vision, why are the young regarded as especially valuable for making needed social changes?
options: They hold the most advanced articulated knowledge and are the least habituated to the institutions and beliefs blamed for society's ills
They are trained in the latest knowledge and are therefore the readiest to defer to whatever practices prevail in society
They retain a natural prudence, untouched by the compromises of adult life, that long experience gradually wears away
They are new enough to public affairs to absorb the accumulated wisdom of the ages faster than their elders can revise their settled opinions

items.stem: The constrained vision concedes that a suitably chosen body of experts may be in the best position to command all the best scientific knowledge available. On its own reasoning, why does this concession not make such experts the proper guides of social decisions?
options: Much of the knowledge that matters is dispersed in unique pieces, usable only if the decisions depending on them are left to those who hold them
Social decisions belong to the democratic majority of contemporaries, whose combined numbers outweigh whatever specialized knowledge an expert body commands
Expert knowledge amounts to fashionable but insignificant words that have little bearing on the practical running of a society's everyday affairs
A cultivated mind can apply reason directly to the facts at hand, so no reasoning individual has any need to defer to a body of experts at all

items.stem: In the constrained vision, when a plain husbandman proves more prudent in managing his own affairs than a Privy Counselor proves in managing other men's, the gap is generally traced to the counselor's inferior natural ability.
options: True
False

items.stem: The constrained vision may grant that a young person just out of school is trained in the latest and most advanced knowledge. Why does it nevertheless refuse to look to the young for leadership in social affairs?
options: The young remain, in its view, a downtrodden group whose judgment was formed under the suppleness and timidity of their fathers
The guide it relies on is prudence, together with a hard-won incredulity, and both are acquired only through experience over time
Its conception of knowledge counts only what has been consciously reasoned out, and the young have had less time to reason things out
The latest forms of knowledge are, in its view, the likeliest to be mistaken, since the age of a belief is itself the best evidence of its soundness

items.stem: Sowell separates two meanings of reason: a cause-and-effect meaning (there is a reason water expands when it freezes, whether or not anyone can say what it is) and an articulated meaning (the specification of causation or logic that is demanded when actions must be justified 'before the bar of reason'). According to Sowell, how does the relationship between these two meanings change across the spectrum of visions?
options: The two coincide at one end of the spectrum and never overlap at the other
The gap between them shrinks as a vision becomes more constrained
The gap between them is the same at every point on the spectrum
The gap between them grows as a vision becomes more constrained

items.stem: True or false: According to Sowell, at the more unconstrained end of the spectrum the two meanings of reason overlap so much that to say a reason for something exists is virtually to say that we can specify it.
options: True
False

items.stem: Sowell writes that, in the constrained vision, an uncontrolled market 'can be analyzed as a general process of interaction with its own characteristic patterns and results' — yet 'cannot be specified in such concrete detail' as to let any individual or group plan or control it. What distinction is he drawing?
options: A process whose patterns can be described can be directed once enough of its detail is gathered
Economists can understand the market's patterns, whereas the participants themselves cannot
A process can have describable patterns without being specifiable in enough detail to direct
The market's patterns become describable only after the fact, never while they are unfolding

items.stem: Sowell says that in the constrained vision of a market, 'the much-vexed question as to just how rational man is has little relevance.' Why does that question carry so little weight in this vision?
options: The constrained vision assumes actors are rational enough for the question to have been settled already
The rationality of the process is systemic, so the rationality of its individual actors is largely incidental
The constrained vision denies that there is any reason at all behind the outcomes a market produces
The constrained vision holds that a market process cannot be analysed, so nothing can be said about rationality

items.stem: For a decade, students at a large university have sold used bicycles through a student-run listing board: each seller posts a price and lowers it until the bike sells. A behavioural-economics class surveys two hundred sellers and finds that most anchor on what they originally paid, few can say why they cut a price when they do, and the group as a whole scores poorly on a standard reasoning test. The class's report concludes that a board run by people who reason this badly cannot be trusted with pricing and should be replaced by a condition-based price table. On Sowell's constrained vision, how much weight does the survey carry against the board?
options: Moderate
Decisive
Little
Considerable

items.stem: On the wards of a regional hospital, nurses have for years covered staffing gaps by trading shifts among themselves through a group chat; no policy governs it. Four proposals reach the board. The risk office, backed by the most senior nurses, wants every trade approved in advance on a written reason, so that coverage rests on accountable judgment. The analytics team, whose model reproduces 94 percent of last year's trades, wants the model to assign coverage directly. A board member wants the analytics study stopped, on the ground that nursing judgment cannot be reduced to a spreadsheet. The chief nurse simply wants the trades left alone. Which proposal does Sowell's constrained vision favour?
options: Stop the analytics study
Approve each trade on a written reason
Leave the trades as they are
Assign coverage from the model

items.stem: A regional bakery chain's thirty store managers each set the next day's bake. Head office's forecaster, a former statistics professor, sends a lucid weekly memo that explains the week's demand and gives each store its quantities; managers praise the memo and say they read it closely. Their actual quantities, though, drift from her figures in different directions store by store, and when asked why, each names something different — a school calendar, a road closure, a regular customer's habits. Chain-wide waste has been among the lowest in the industry for a decade. The CEO credits the forecaster for that record and proposes making her figures binding. On Sowell's constrained vision, where does the wisdom behind the chain's low waste lie?
options: In the managers' explanations
In head office's coordination
In the forecaster's memos
In the managers' adjustments

items.stem: According to Sowell, how do those holding the unconstrained vision see the conflict over judicial activism?
options: As a contest between the democratic majority of the present generation and an unelected court that would set aside that majority's preferences
As a contest between two sets of contemporaries, or at most between the living and one dead generation that has no right to rule beyond the grave
As a contest between the original meanings of the Constitution's words and the fresh meanings a later court would propose to read into them
As a contest between the accumulated experience of successive generations, carried by one living group, and the articulated reasoning of their contemporary opponents

items.stem: Sowell presents the constrained vision's resistance to judicial activism as essentially a defense of one particular past generation, the Founding Fathers, against the judgment of the present one.
options: True
False

items.stem: An advocate of an activist court argues that the real question is whether today's citizens must live under the judgment of a generation that died two centuries ago. According to Sowell, how would a jurist of the constrained vision, such as Holmes, recast that question?
options: As whether the experience distilled across many generations is wiser than the reasoning of any one group, living or dead
As whether the framers who wrote the constitutional text were wiser than the most cultivated legal minds of the present generation
As whether the original meaning of the constitutional text is wiser than the fresh moral insight a judge would read into it
As whether a democratic majority of living contemporaries is wiser than the unelected judges who would override its preferences

items.stem: Mill insisted that laws are made, not evolved, and dismissed deference to precedent as sacrificing present ends to antiquated means. Why does Sowell nonetheless decline to treat him as a clear-cut spokesman for the unconstrained vision on law?
options: His provisos, that lawmakers reckon with what the people will bear, their ancient habits, and continuity in institutions, bring him close to Hayek's claim that early lawgivers merely articulated existing practice
He wrote before the modern controversy over judicial activism had taken shape, so Sowell reads his remarks on made-versus-grown law as a historical aside rather than a commitment to either vision

He later came around to Holmes's account of the law developing like a planet, each generation taking the next step, and withdrew his description of evolved law as a fortuitous concourse of atoms in ages of barbarism

He conceded that the laws of Moses and of Mahomet grew rather than being made, which placed the most ancient legal codes on the constrained side of the very distinction he had drawn between made and evolved law

items.stem: Sowell observes that advocates of judicial activism such as Dworkin dismiss the claims of prior generations. According to Sowell, on what ground do they claim the authority to reshape the law?
options: The reasoned and revocable will of today's living majority, which ought not to be bound by any idealized ancestral compulsion
An intellectually and morally superior decision process, competent to override even a democratic majority of contemporaries
The spontaneous growth of the law itself, in which each generation takes the next step beyond the one before
Contemporary circumstances that have moved far beyond the wisdom of even the wisest of the Founding Fathers

items.stem: According to the chapter, what does the constrained vision hold to be each individual's best contribution to society?
options: Bringing his expertise to bear on whichever public question he judges to be the most pressing
Pursuing the public good sincerely in every decision that his position allows him to make
Striving to shape the best outcome in each particular issue that comes within his own jurisdiction
Adhering to the special duties of his institutional role, leaving outcomes to systemic processes

items.stem: True or false: According to the chapter, the constrained vision can admit that a chief justice is better than anyone else at determining how the written law applies to a case, and still hold that whether the result is right or good is not his business.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter says the constrained vision regards 'social responsibility' in business — hiring the disadvantaged, investing where society seems to need it most, giving part of the proceeds to charity — as outside the businessman's competence. Why?
options: Executives who claim to serve the public are presumed to be insincere, so any aim they state beyond profit deserves no weight at all
Their wider effects run through a systemic process he cannot trace; the social benefit comes from competition, not his intentions
Society's needs are better judged by public officials, whose knowledge of them is far broader than any single businessman's could be
The law confines a firm's resources to its owners' profit, so social aims of that kind are simply not his to pursue with the firm's money

items.stem: True or false: Because a judge's position and a business executive's serve different ends, the constrained vision judges the two by different standards — the judge by how faithfully he applies the law, the executive by how much benefit his firm produces for society.
options: True
False
justify_options: Neither has the competence to judge the social good case by case, so each serves it by keeping to his post and leaving results to the process
An executive's benefit to society cannot be measured at all, whereas a judge's fidelity to the law can be checked on appeal by a higher court
Producing benefit for society is a task for government, not for firms, so an executive is measured only by the profit he returns to his owners

items.stem: Priya Raman runs a regional trucking company. A customer offers a large and unusually profitable contract whose delivery schedule could be met only by keeping drivers on the road beyond the legal limit on hours behind the wheel; the violations would almost certainly never be detected. Priya declines, the quarter's profit falls, and she tells the board she will not make money by breaking a rule that other people on the road depend on. Two directors call it a fine gesture the company cannot afford. A third has argued for years that a company's contribution to society comes from competing for its own gain, not from its managers' good intentions, and that he distrusts any manager who talks of serving the public. What verdict on Priya's decision follows from the third director's position?
options: Doing her job
Failing the owners
Overstepping her job
Erring in good faith

items.stem: Professor Idris Bello runs a seminar on housing policy. He is convinced that rent control harms the very tenants it is meant to protect, and he assigns the readings and sequences the discussions so that students arrive at that conclusion by the end of term; he says openly that this is the point of the course. A colleague objects that a seminar should lay out the evidence on both sides and leave students to decide. Which verdict on Idris follows from the unconstrained vision?
options: Right in aim, wrong in method
Teaching as he should
Indoctrinating, not teaching
Right only if his view is sound

items.stem: Judge Amara Whitfield hears the appeal of a small bakery fined under a state food-labelling statute. She is convinced that rules of this kind are strangling small firms and that the state would be better off with fewer of them. The statute's wording plainly reaches the bakery, and it contains no exception for small businesses. She rules for the bakery, holding that the legislature 'cannot have intended' to reach a firm this size, and describes her ruling as a narrow reading that keeps the state's power in check. Which verdict on the ruling follows from the constrained vision?
options: A misuse of the bench
Overdue relief for small firms
A forgivable stretch
Restraint, properly exercised

items.stem: According to the chapter, which practice is characteristic of how adherents of the unconstrained vision have treated their adversaries?
options: Attributing their errors to the complexity of the social process itself
Conceding their sincerity as an individual virtue of minor social benefit
Referring to the adversaries' "real" reasons, which must be "unmasked"
Granting that they may do the worst of things without being the worst of men

items.stem: In the constrained vision, as the chapter presents it, an adversary's sincerity can count as a major aggravating factor rather than a point in his favor, when he persists in socially counterproductive ideals.
options: True
False

items.stem: The chapter observes that adherents of the constrained vision concede sincerity to their adversaries more readily than adherents of the unconstrained vision do. Why?
options: Because sincerity weighs so little in their vision that conceding it costs them almost nothing
Because they regard their adversaries' reasoning as too feeble to pose any serious challenge
Because their case rests on unarticulated experience, which no adversary's argument can touch
Because they take a more charitable view of their adversaries' character than their opponents do

items.stem: Godwin's version of the unconstrained vision holds that neither deception nor force is justified in pursuing the public good, while Lenin's version makes them duties. According to the chapter, what produces this difference?
options: Whether each is willing to trust the naturally evolved systemic processes of society
Whether each places the wisest and most beneficent far above most people of their time
How much weight each attaches to the individual's sincerity and dedication to the common good
How much friction each assumes reason must overcome on the way to winning public assent

items.stem: The chapter says the constrained vision's rationale for fidelity to truth is very similar to its rationale for fidelity to roles. What do the two have in common?
options: Each treats honesty as a single virtue in which sincerity and fidelity carry equal weight in either vision
Each derives from articulated canons of reason that any sufficiently cultivated mind is able to specify
Each rests on the individual's competence to determine directly what would serve society in the case at hand
Each yields one's own judgment of the case at hand to a broader process trusted for its long-run results

learning_objectives.1.1: Identify the kinds of evidence Flynn offers for his claim that Singapore delivers the world's best healthcare at the world's lowest cost — published outcome rankings, per-person spending comparisons, and a week of first-hand observation undertaken because the numbers seemed too good to be true to a self-described cynical economist.
learning_objectives.1.2: Explain what Flynn's pairing of outcome rankings with spending comparisons is meant to establish: that the United States pays far more per person than Singapore and still trails it on every outcome he cites, so the gap is a failure on both axes rather than a price-for-quality trade-off — and that the countries usually offered as US models, Canada and the United Kingdom, also spend far more than Singapore.
learning_objectives.1.3: Explain how, on Flynn's reading, the cabbie's complaint that he has to go to the gym because he would bear much of the cost of developing diabetes is evidence the system works rather than a flaw: personal cost exposure, explicitly not a government mandate, produces the sustained preventive effort US professionals mostly just talk about.
learning_objectives.1.4: Explain why Flynn treats the US origin of Singapore's components — price tags and health savings accounts, developed in America decades earlier — together with their use by Whole Foods and by Indiana, as answering his opening question of whether the approach could work back home: the US merely invented, while Singapore implemented.
learning_objectives.1.5: Explain why Flynn expects reform on Singapore's model to be thankless but not fruitless: beneficiaries stop perceiving a good system and complain about the very incentives that make it work, while the payoff he claims accrues whether or not anyone notices.

Chapter 1 → The Cabbie's Tale.text: A sceptical economist flew out for a week because the reported pairing of top results with the lowest spending seemed implausible. He found a well-run neighbourhood clinic whose staff saw nothing remarkable in it, and a driver who resented exercising because he would meet much of the cost of falling ill — pressure no rule imposed. The components, he notes, were American inventions that another country merely applied. Reform, he predicts, would go uncredited without going unrewarded.

items.stem: According to the chapter, why did Flynn fly to Singapore to examine its healthcare system in person?
options: No published figures on Singapore's system existed, so he had to gather the basic data himself.
He was convinced the statistics were false and went to document the system's hidden flaws.
The statistics he had read seemed too good to be true, and he wanted to confirm they were not lying.
Singapore's health ministry had invited him on an official visit to evaluate its neighborhood polyclinics.

items.stem: According to the chapter, on what kinds of evidence does Flynn rest his claim that Singapore delivers the world's best healthcare at the world's lowest cost?
options: Published outcome rankings, a week of observing the system himself, and cost projections from his own economic model.
Published outcome rankings, per-person spending comparisons, and the results of Whole Foods' and Indiana's programs.
Published outcome rankings, per-person spending comparisons, and a week of observing the system himself.
A week of observing the system himself, per-person spending comparisons, and an official evaluation by its health ministry.

items.stem: Flynn reports gathering first-hand evidence during his week in Singapore. According to the chapter, which of the following was part of that effort?
options: Meeting the health ministry's leadership to review the government's own official outcome statistics.
Comparing the annual budgets of several polyclinics with those of comparable clinics in the United States.
Touring the country's leading private hospitals rather than its government-run neighborhood clinics.
Asking doctors, former public health officials, cabbies, and shop clerks what they thought of the system.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the Bloomberg Businessweek ranking Flynn cites is presumably a measure of per-person healthcare spending rather than of health outcomes.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, how does per-person healthcare spending in the United States compare with Singapore's?
options: The US spends about one and a half times as much per person as Singapore.
The US and Singapore spend about the same amount per person on healthcare.
The US spends somewhat less per person than Singapore does.
The US spends nearly three times as much per person as Singapore.

items.stem: According to the chapter, the United States edges out Singapore on at least one of the three measures of healthcare effectiveness that Flynn calls most important, even though it trails on the others.
options: True
False

items.stem: Flynn presents Singapore's outcome rankings alongside per-person spending comparisons. According to the chapter, what is that pairing meant to establish about the United States?
options: That its extra spending buys strengths the three headline measures miss and only a broader index can reveal.
That its results would rise to Singapore's level if it were willing to spend more per person on healthcare.
That Singapore's low spending is offset by weaker results on some measures, so each country trades price against quality.
That it pays far more than Singapore yet gets worse results, so the gap is not a matter of paying more for better care.

items.stem: Suppose Flynn had reported only the outcome rankings, with the United States trailing Singapore on each measure, and said nothing about spending. According to the chapter's line of argument, which reply to Flynn's case would that leave open?
options: That the outcome statistics are too good to be true and cannot be taken at face value.
That the US is simply spending less than Singapore and getting the level of care it pays for.
That Singapore's results rest on policies foreign to the US that could not be transplanted here.
That the three measures are too narrow to judge a whole system, so the ranking proves little on its own.

items.stem: According to the chapter, why does Flynn extend the spending comparison beyond the United States to Canada and the United Kingdom?
options: They spend about what Singapore spends per person, which leaves the United States as the lone high-cost outlier.
They rank ahead of Singapore on Bloomberg's broader index, which makes them the fairer benchmark for outcomes.
They, rather than the United States, developed the price tags and savings accounts Singapore later implemented.
They are the usual models offered for US reform, and even they spend far more per person than Singapore.

items.stem: According to the chapter, how did Flynn react once the cabbie explained why he hated Singapore's healthcare system?
options: He pressed the cabbie for other flaws that outsiders might have missed
He smiled, taking what the cabbie called a problem to be an answer
He told the cabbie that regular exercise was a small price for his health
He noted the complaint as his first sign that the statistics had been oversold

items.stem: According to the chapter, when Flynn asked whether the government forced him to go to the gym, the cabbie said no; he went because he would have to pay much of the cost himself if he got fat and developed diabetes.
options: True
False

items.stem: On Flynn's reading, why does the cabbie's complaint count as evidence that Singapore's system is working rather than as a report of a flaw in it?
options: What he resents is an exercise rule that the government applies evenly to every citizen
What he resents is trivial next to the treatment costs he would otherwise face
What he resents is the sort of thing people find to complain about under any arrangement
What he resents is the sustained preventive effort the system exists to produce

items.stem: According to the chapter, what struck Flynn about the cabbie's habit was that Singapore had found a way to get an ordinary citizen to comply with a government exercise requirement, something US healthcare professionals had only talked about doing.
options: True
False

items.stem: A delivery company changes one thing about breakdowns: when a van fails on its route from a fault the driver could have caught on a morning walkaround, the tow and the lost day come out of that driver's quarterly bonus. Six months in, a consultant asks four drivers what they think of it. Ben: 'I hate it. Since the bonus thing my supervisor has us sign a twenty-point sheet every morning, and I do every line, because he is at the gate checking twice a week.' Cal: 'I hate it. In March a fuel pump quit on me halfway through my route, no warning at all, and the tow and the lost day came out of my bonus anyway.' Ana: 'I hate it. Belts, hoses, tires, my own routine now, every day before I pull out. It beats paying for a tow, but I have been late to my first stop twice.' Dee: 'It's fine. The shop fixes things properly now instead of patching them, my van has not been off the road once all year, and it has never cost me a cent.' Which driver's response is the counterpart of the cabbie's in Flynn's chapter?
options: Cal
Ana
Dee
Ben

items.stem: A housing co-op has long paid for burst-pipe repairs out of its shared reserve and has run a well-attended winterizing workshop every October. Two years ago the board changed one thing about billing: a unit now pays for repairs to its own frozen pipes. The workshop continues. At this year's annual meeting a resident who says she has no interest in home maintenance tells the board she hates the change, because every October she now has to crawl under her deck to shut off the outside tap and drain the line. She adds that the workshop taught her how years ago. Several neighbors nod. The board asks what to do. If the board reasons about her the way Flynn reasons about the cabbie, what does it do?
options: Drop the billing change and expand the workshop
Leave the billing change and the workshop as they are
Make the October shutoff a bylaw with a fine for missing it
Return frozen-pipe repairs to the shared reserve

items.stem: Four colleges at one university want final grades submitted on time. At Ashby a late grade sheet costs the instructor a hundred dollars a day, itemized as a line on the next pay stub, and instructors grumble that they now drop everything in exam week. At Bell nothing is deducted; the registrar no longer covers for late grades, so a late instructor sorts out every resulting enrollment hold, and instructors grumble that they now drop everything in exam week. At Cole the dean circulates a memo every term on the importance of timeliness and presents a plaque to the most punctual department at the faculty meeting, and instructors grumble about the memo. At Dunn a staff member in the records office quietly handles whatever late grades produce, as she has for years; nobody is charged and nothing is said, and instructors do not grumble at all. A visiting economist who reasons as Flynn does about the cabbie is asked which college has built what the cabbie was describing. Which does she name?
options: Cole
Ashby
Bell
Dunn

items.stem: According to the chapter, where does Flynn say the major components of Singapore's healthcare system, such as price tags and health savings accounts, were originally developed?
options: In Canada and the United Kingdom, the countries often proposed as models for US reform
In the United States, in many cases decades before Singapore made use of them
In the United States, but only recently and in response to Singapore's results
In Singapore, by officials designing a system to suit its own population

items.stem: According to the chapter, when Flynn says the United States 'merely invented, while Singapore implemented,' the inventions he has in mind are mainly medical technologies, such as drugs and devices, that Singapore then adopted.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, Flynn went to Singapore wanting to know, among other things, whether what it was doing 'might also work back home.' After returning, he discovered that Singapore's major components had originally been developed in the United States. How does Flynn treat that discovery in relation to his question?
options: As answering it yes: the ideas are already American and should have produced the result here first, so all that is missing is implementation
As answering it no: Singapore succeeded only by reworking American ideas that had already failed at home, so re-importing them would repeat that failure
As changing it: since the ideas were American, Flynn argues the United States deserves the credit for Singapore's results rather than needing to copy them
As leaving it open: who invented a policy says nothing about whether it works, so Flynn falls back on the outcome statistics to settle the question

items.stem: According to the chapter, having argued that Singapore's components were invented in America, Flynn then points to Whole Foods Market and to former Indiana governors as Americans who, he says, have already implemented such policies. What work does this citation do in his argument?
options: It supplies his main evidence: detailed cost and outcome figures from these programmes, which replace the Singapore statistics as proof
It concedes a limit: private firms and state governments can adopt such policies, but Flynn doubts a national system could
It names the inventors: Flynn credits Mackey, Daniels and Pence with originally developing price tags and health savings accounts
It moves the claim from 'could work here' to 'has already been done here': Americans can implement, not only invent

items.stem: According to the chapter, Flynn writes that the United States 'merely invented, while Singapore implemented.' Which reading best captures the contrast he is drawing?
options: The policies were developed in America as voluntary options, while Singapore made them work by having the government compel their use
The policies were developed in America but never used to build its healthcare system, while Singapore built its system on them
The policies were developed in America in rough form, and only Singapore's later refinements turned them into something that could work
The policies were developed in America and adopted in both countries, but Singapore has run them more effectively than the United States

items.stem: At the close of the chapter, Flynn tells anyone who signs on to implement Singapore-style reform in the United States what to expect. According to the chapter, what does he predict?
options: Reform will probably be fruitless, but reformers would still be thanked.
Reform will probably be thankless, but it won't be fruitless.
Reform will be appreciated once Americans notice how much better it is.
Reform will be resisted until the government mandates regular exercise.

items.stem: According to the chapter, Flynn expects that a few years after a Singapore-style reform took effect, most Americans would probably remember how bad the old system had been and thank the reformers for the change.
options: True
False

items.stem: Flynn closes the chapter by predicting that reform on Singapore's model would probably be 'thankless' but would not be 'fruitless.' According to the chapter, what distinction is he drawing?
options: Whether Americans invent the components is separate from whether they implement them.
Whether the reform pays off depends on whether people notice and appreciate it.
Whether people complain about the reform shows whether it has failed to deliver.
Whether people credit the reform is separate from whether it delivers its benefits.

items.stem: Flynn writes that 'a fish doesn't know that it's living in water,' and earlier he describes a senior polyclinic nurse who could not understand why anybody would be impressed by her clinic. According to the chapter, what point do these two illustrations make?
options: People complain about a system's incentives even when the incentives work.
People who benefit from a well-run system stop noticing how good it is.
People resent being photographed or studied by outsiders.
People in poor neighborhoods have access to modern, well-run public clinics.

items.stem: In his closing prediction, Flynn writes that, 'as with my cabbie in Singapore, people will find things to complain about.' According to the chapter, what does invoking the cabbie add to his prediction that reform would be thankless?
options: Some beneficiaries would find genuine flaws in the system that outsiders cannot see.
Some beneficiaries would need a government mandate before they changed their habits.
Some beneficiaries would resent the very incentives that make the system work.
Some beneficiaries would stop noticing the system because they were used to it.

learning_objectives.2.1: Explain how the chapter establishes that Singapore's rise since independence was exceptional: the reversal of its standing relative to the United States, matched by comparable gains in health and environment, and its ranking as the richest nation once oil, banking and gambling economies are set aside.
learning_objectives.2.2: Explain how the chapter makes the PAP's electoral dominance the enabling condition for Lee's long-horizon policymaking, including the feedback loop by which policy success extended that dominance.
learning_objectives.2.3: Explain how meritocratic schooling and integrated, owner-occupied public housing were designed to give every ethnic and religious group an equal chance at advancement and a real stake in the economy.
learning_objectives.2.4: Apply Lee's carrot-and-stick logic for escaping the middle-income trap to a novel case, predicting whether a proposed policy pairing would make low-productivity production unprofitable enough to push firms to upgrade.
learning_objectives.2.5: Explain the role of the Central Provident Fund in Singapore's development: how compulsory saving at high combined rates supplied domestic capital in place of borrowing from foreign investors, and why Lee put its investment under engineers and technocrats rather than bankers.
learning_objectives.2.6: Explain how Singapore's tax design — low, flat, almost no deductions, with credits only for research and development, training, high-efficiency equipment and intellectual property — makes innovation, investment and entrepreneurship the only route by which a firm can reduce its taxable income.

Chapter 2 → The Colony of Singapore.text: A trading settlement founded under a British company in the early nineteenth century, drawing labourers from China and elsewhere, it prospered by sitting at the narrow point every east-west voyage through the region must pass. Independence arrived late and poor, with income per head roughly a fifth of the American figure. Within half a century that relationship had inverted, and among countries with varied economies none was richer.

Chapter 2 → Rich, Green, and Prosperous.text: Gains were not confined to income. Where cholera and typhoid once circulated and waste ran untreated into the water, the city is now unusually clean and densely planted, topping assessments of urban greenery. Most residents own their homes, a far larger share than in America, and a tenth of households hold wealth above a million dollars, behind only an oil state and a banking centre.

Chapter 2 → How Did Things Get So Good?.text: The explanation offered is governance. The governing party won by margins wide enough, on this account, to free the first prime minister from bargaining with rivals, factions or interest groups, leaving him to pick whichever policies he judged best. Success then made that party more popular still and secured further terms — a loop the chapter credits with letting ministers spend their time solving problems rather than campaigning, and so plan further ahead.

Chapter 2 → Policies for Prosperity?.text: Schooling was made excellent and advancement made to follow measured achievement, so every community shared one route upward. Flats were built with subsidy and then sold rather than let, with quotas keeping each block mixed, which gave residents both an asset and a stake. To escape stalling at low-wage manufacturing, owners were offered generous help buying better machinery and training staff, while a charge on wages made staying cheap unprofitable.

Chapter 2 → Savings and Wealth.text: A compulsory savings scheme, the Central Provident Fund, was inherited from the colonial administration and expanded until worker and employer each put in a quarter of pay — an extraordinary rate by rich-world standards. That pool funded roads, schools and firms, sparing the country dependence on foreign lenders, and engineers rather than financiers were entrusted with investing it. Taxes stayed low and flat, with relief only for research, training, equipment and intellectual property.

Agriculture and resource extraction, unable to industrialise at all
Light industry, unable to move on to heavy or high-tech industry

items.stem: On Lee's logic as the chapter presents it, why did the wage surtax lead low-productivity factory owners to accept the upgrade subsidies rather than carry on as before?
options: It made carrying on without the subsidies a breach of the law
A steady supply of well-educated graduates made upgrading easy
It raised labour costs until the low-tech factory no longer paid
It funded the subsidies from the pockets of the low-wage firms themselves

items.stem: On Lee's logic as the chapter presents it, the subsidies for higher-tech equipment and worker training were arguably enough on their own to move light-industry owners off low-productivity production.
options: True
False

items.stem: A hospital group buys laundered linen and sterile packs from a network of small local suppliers, most of which still run labour-intensive operations on low pay. The group announces the largest supplier programme in its history: it will pay most of the cost of automated washing and packing lines for any supplier that wants them, and will train the supplier's staff to run the new equipment. The offer is open for a fixed window, after which it closes for good. Suppliers that decline stay on their current contracts at current prices. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what should the group expect most of its suppliers to do?
options: Drop out of the network
Keep running as they are
Automate as the window closes
Take the offer and automate

items.stem: A port authority licenses a dozen private firms to load and unload cargo on its quays. Most still work the old way, with large gangs of low-paid casual labour rather than the container cranes and automated yards used at rival ports. The authority announces the toughest package it has ever adopted: a charge on every hour of low-paid casual labour worked on the quays, large enough that the old way stops paying, together with a well-funded scheme, open to dockworkers rather than to the firms, that retrains anyone whose job disappears and places them with other employers. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what should the authority expect most of the firms to do?
options: Buy cranes at their own cost
Buy cranes using the scheme
Carry on and pay the charge
Hand back their licences

items.stem: In the weaving district of Orlan, in the country of Halveria, most workshops still run hand-fed looms with low-paid operators. The district council adopts two measures at once. The first is a grant covering most of the cost of modern looms and of training operators to run them. The second, the first of its kind in the district's history, is a levy on every hour of low-paid work; the workshop owners' association has denounced it as an attack on the trade. The levy is set at the level needed to cover the council's cost of processing grant applications. Applying the chapter's reasoning, what should the council expect most workshops to do?
options: Re-equip without the grant
Close rather than re-equip
Take the grant and re-equip
Carry on as they are

items.stem: According to the chapter, how did the Central Provident Fund (CPF) come into being, and what was Lee Kuan Yew's part in it?
options: It began as a program of the Malaysian federation, which Singapore kept after its expulsion, leaving the contribution rates as they were.
The Housing and Development Board created it to finance apartment construction, and Lee later widened it to retirement saving.
Lee created it shortly after full independence, as one of his first economic measures, and set its contribution rates high from the outset.
It was set up under British colonial administration, before independence; Lee's contribution was to raise its rates over time.

items.stem: According to the chapter, how did the savings rate produced by the CPF's peak contribution rates compare with the personal savings rate of the United States?
options: It roughly matched the highest US rate of the postwar decades, but Singapore sustained that level for far longer than the United States did.
It fell short of the peak US rate, because contributions made by employers were not counted as personal saving by the worker.
It was far above the highest rate the United States has ever recorded, and beyond anything Western Europe or Japan has reached.
It exceeded the long-run US average in most years, but stayed below the highest US rates that were recorded over the same period.

items.stem: The chapter calls the cash generated by the CPF 'essential' to Singapore's development. On the chapter's account, why was it essential?
options: It showed foreign investors that Singaporeans were thrifty and disciplined savers, which drew in the foreign capital that financed most of the country's growth.
It guaranteed every worker a retirement income, which relieved the government of having to fund support for the elderly out of general tax revenue.
It gave Singapore its own pool of capital to invest in infrastructure, schools and businesses, instead of the foreign borrowing many poor nations rely on.
It held down household consumption, which kept inflation low enough for the currency to be fully backed by international assets and remain strong.

items.stem: According to the chapter, why did Lee put the CPF's investments in the hands of engineers and technocrats rather than bankers and financiers?
options: He worried bankers would park the money in safe, low-yield reserves, leaving the fund too little growth to pay out workers' retirement benefits when they came due.
He feared bankers would lend the fund's money to borrowers abroad at higher interest, draining away the domestic capital that compulsory saving had been built to accumulate.
He wanted the money steered into productive technologies, infrastructure and education, not into the short-run profits financiers might be tempted to chase.
He expected engineers to estimate the costs of ports, roads and housing more accurately, which would keep the fund's construction projects within their budgets.

items.stem: On the chapter's account, Singapore financed its development in much the same way as many poor nations, largely by borrowing from foreign investors, with the CPF serving mainly as a retirement scheme for its workers.
options: True
False

items.stem: According to the chapter, what is the only way a business in Singapore can reduce its taxable income?
options: By keeping wages low enough to avoid the government's surtax
By engaging in innovation, investment, or entrepreneurship
By claiming the ordinary business deductions the flat tax allows
By paying the required contributions into its workers' CPF accounts

items.stem: According to the chapter, Singapore kept its taxes low in order to attract foreign investment and to let local companies reinvest more of their profits.
options: True
False

items.stem: On the chapter's account, why is engaging in innovation, investment or entrepreneurship the only way a business in Singapore can reduce its taxable income?
options: Because the rates are already so low, firms have little tax left to reduce, and the credits are the only reductions still worth the effort of claiming.
Because the flat tax allows almost no other loopholes or deductions, the credits tied to those activities are the only reductions left to claim.
Because the wage surtax claws back whatever a firm saves through ordinary deductions, the credits are the only reductions that actually survive it.
Because the credits are so generous, firms prefer them to the ordinary business deductions that the code continues to make available to them.

items.stem: On the chapter's account, why is the near-absence of other deductions essential to the incentive? That is, why would the credits for R&D, training, high-efficiency equipment and intellectual property, on their own, not make those activities the only route to a lower taxable income?
options: With ordinary deductions still available, firms would use them to offset the wage surtax and keep their low-productivity factories profitable.
Without closing the other deductions, the code would lose the simplicity and transparency that the chapter says is what draws foreign investors to Singapore.
With ordinary deductions still available, firms could cut taxable income without innovating, and the credited activities would be one option among several.
Without closing the other deductions, the government could not afford credits as generous as the chapter describes, so it would have to scale them back.

items.stem: According to the chapter, what makes innovation, investment and entrepreneurship the only way for a Singapore firm to reduce its taxable income is mainly the low level of its tax rates; the flat structure with almost no deductions serves mostly to keep the system simple and transparent.
options: True
False
